**Video:** [Lec 52 — Transfer Learning and Knowledge Distillation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5f2_TocU_CU)

## Learning goals

- Define **transfer learning**: pretrain on a source task, adapt to a target task with less data.
- Contrast freezing a backbone vs **fine-tuning**.
- Explain **knowledge distillation**: train a student to match a teacher’s soft predictions.

## Before this clicks

Training a huge net from scratch needs lots of labeled data and compute. Often someone already trained a strong model on a related problem (ImageNet, large text corpora). **Transfer** reuses those features. **Distillation** compresses a strong “teacher” into a cheaper “student” by matching soft labels, not only hard one-hot targets.

---

## Main ideas

### 1. Transfer learning pipeline

1. **Pretrain** $f_{\theta}$ on source data (e.g. classify 1000 ImageNet classes).
2. **Adapt** to target data (e.g. medical images with 5 classes): replace / retrain the head, optionally update lower layers.

Intuition: early layers learn generic edges/textures/syntax; later layers are more task-specific.

### 2. Freeze vs fine-tune

| Strategy | What updates | When |
|----------|--------------|------|
| Feature extraction | Only new head | Tiny target data; avoid destroying pretrained features |
| Partial fine-tune | Head + top blocks | Moderate data |
| Full fine-tune | All parameters (small LR) | More target data; domain close enough |

Use a **smaller learning rate** for pretrained weights than for a randomly initialized head.

### 3. Domain shift caveat

If source and target distributions differ wildly, transfer helps less (or needs more fine-tuning / better pretraining). Transfer is a prior, not magic.

### 4. Knowledge distillation (KD)

Teacher $T$ (large, frozen or slowly updated) produces soft probabilities $p_T(y\mid x)$. Student $S$ with parameters $\phi$ matches them.

Temperature-softmax (Hinton et al.):

$$
p^{(T)}_c(x)=\frac{\exp(z_c/T)}{\sum_{c'}\exp(z_{c'}/T)},
$$

where $z_c$ are logits and $T>1$ softens the distribution (reveals “dark knowledge”: which wrong classes are near-misses).

Student loss (schematic):

$$
L(\phi)=(1-\lambda)\,L_{\mathrm{hard}}\big(y,p_S\big)
+\lambda\,T^{2}\,L_{\mathrm{KD}}\big(p_T^{(T)},p_S^{(T)}\big),
$$

where $L_{\mathrm{KD}}$ is often KL divergence between teacher and student soft labels, and $T^{2}$ rescales gradients when temperature is used. $\lambda\in[0,1]$ balances hard labels vs teacher mimicry.

### 5. Why distill?

Deploy a small/fast student on-device while keeping much of the teacher’s accuracy. Same idea appears when compressing ensembles into one net.

---

## Worked mini-example

Teacher on a 3-class problem outputs soft probs $(0.70,0.25,0.05)$ for an image whose hard label is class 0. Hard-label training only says “class 0.” Distillation also tells the student “class 1 is more plausible than class 2,” transferring similarity structure. With $T>1$ those $(0.70,0.25,0.05)$ become even flatter, emphasizing relative structure over peaky confidence.

---

## Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Transfer = always freeze everything | Freezing is one mode; fine-tuning often works better with enough data. |
| Distillation needs unlabeled data only | You can mix hard labels and soft teacher targets; setups vary. |
| Student must share teacher architecture | Architectures may differ; student is usually smaller. |
| Soft labels = temperature alone | Temperature reshapes logits; the teacher network produces the logits. |
